name: callback
intent: Pass executable code plus per-operation context to a provider that owns when work completes, so it can deliver a result, error or event without coupling to the caller's concrete type; use it only with a documented invocation contract covering timing, cardinality, execution context and lifetime.
problem: An operation's outcome is not available at initiation—or a framework must invoke caller-supplied behavior at a lifecycle or event boundary—so a return value cannot carry it. Blocking burns a thread, polling adds latency, and provider-specific knowledge couples the service to each caller. The design must make timing (inline or deferred), cardinality (once or repeated), execution context, lifetime and cancellation, and error delivery explicit; otherwise callbacks can re-enter unexpectedly, fire after teardown, or lose failures.
context: Use this pattern when an operation cannot complete within the call that starts it or when a framework owns an event or lifecycle boundary: asynchronous I/O and network clients, timers and schedulers, UI/event loops, plugin hooks, and generic algorithms that take behaviour as an argument. An immediate callback such as a qsort comparator runs during the initiating call; a deferred callback such as a Node.js I/O completion runs after it returns; a React setState completion callback runs after a commit. All forms need an explicit contract for ownership, invocation thread, reentrancy, error delivery and cardinality. The deferred form is the primary focus of this record; synchronous callbacks have no deferred lifetime but still need a clear ordering and exception contract.
benefits: Non-blocking initiation: the caller's thread is not held for the duration of the work, so one thread can drive many operations that are in flight at the same time.
Decoupling through inversion of control: the service depends only on the callback's signature, never on the concrete client type, so the same service serves every caller.
Behaviour becomes a parameter: generic algorithms and frameworks are reused with per-site behaviour (comparators, iteration and folding callbacks, lifecycle hooks).
The callback and its context are the rendezvous point for results that cannot be returned: completion status, payload, progress reports and errors all travel through one signature.
One callback per operation demultiplexes many concurrent operations without a shared completion queue — the client can distinguish them by the context it passed in.
Polling disappears: the callee signals completion exactly when it happens, so latency is bounded by the work rather than by the poll interval.
Dual invocation modes: callbacks work equally well for one-shot completions (async I/O) and repeated events (DOM listeners, emitters), unlike promises which model a single future value.
tradeoffs: Inversion of control obscures the flow: completion is not visible where the work was started, stack traces end in the dispatcher, and debuggers stop in framework code rather than at the call site.

Execution context is now a design question: the callback may run on another thread, inside the dispatcher loop, in a signal or interrupt context, or re-enter the service — shared state and blocking calls must be designed for that.

Lifetime and ownership become explicit burdens: the callback and everything it captured must outlive the operation (dangling void* context in C, retained self in Swift, bound-method cycles in Python, strong listener references in Java/C#, borrow and 'static constraints in Rust).

Errors need an invented convention: an exception raised by the callback cannot travel back to the initiator, so each realization relies on an errback/status/failed-path argument and any path that forgets it loses the failure silently.

Cancellation and unregistration are extra design: after the client stops caring the callback can still fire, so a handle plus defined post-cancel semantics are needed to avoid double completion, late side effects or leaks.

No composition: sequencing more than one or two asynchronous steps turns into nesting, and ordering, timeouts, retries, backpressure and fan-in have to be re-invented — which is why promises, futures and coroutines were introduced.

The callback contract is not self-documenting: unlike a returned Future or Promise, there is no type-level indication of whether the callback fires once or many times, synchronously or asynchronously, and on which thread.

participants.responsibility: Issues the operation, supplies the callback and the per-operation context, and continues without waiting for the result.
The executable code (function pointer, interface implementation, closure, delegate, block) that receives completion, progress and failures; one method or a small set such as success/failure.
Receives the callback and its context, performs the work that cannot finish before returning, and invokes the callback according to the contract when the work completes or progresses.
Carries the per-operation state the callback needs when it finally runs (client object, request identity, buffers), because the initiating stack frame no longer exists.
The thread, loop or runtime on which the callback is finally invoked; it fixes synchronous versus deferred invocation and supplies the threading and reentrancy guarantees.

use_cases: Non-blocking I/O: Node.js fs.readFile and Boost.Asio async operations hand a result or error to a completion handler; the provider must document its dispatcher, cancellation and exactly-once semantics (Swift URLSession and Python asyncio use analogous contracts).
Timers and schedulers: run this code later or repeatedly (setTimeout/setInterval, loop.call_later, threading.Timer, DispatchSourceTimer).
Event handling: an event source (DOM, UI toolkit, message bus, actor runtime) invokes registered handlers when events arrive (addEventListener, .NET events, Java listener lists, signal handlers).

Algorithms parameterized by behaviour: the C qsort comparator, Go sort.Slice less function, Array.prototype.forEach and Ruby blocks run supplied code during the initiating call, so they are synchronous callbacks with no deferred lifetime.
Progress and streaming notifications: deliver partial results as they arrive (IProgress<T>, progress callbacks, chunked receive callbacks).
Fan-in over many in-flight operations: one completion callback per request lets a client correlate and aggregate responses (pairs with Asynchronous Completion Token and Return Address).
Framework extension points and plugins: the framework calls registered hooks at fixed moments (before/after hooks, middleware, lifecycle callbacks, interceptors).
Continuation-Passing Style (CPS): chain asynchronous operations where each step passes its result directly to the next callback, the historical basis for async/await desugaring.
Deferred rendering and animation: UI frameworks invoke callbacks after layout or paint passes complete (requestAnimationFrame, layout callbacks).
Bridge to foreign runtimes: callbacks are the lingua franca for crossing async boundaries between languages and environments (JS engine callbacks from native code, Python ctypes, Rust FFI).
Streams and pipelines: chunked data sources invoke the same callback repeatedly as each chunk arrives (ReadableStream, fs.createReadStream, RxJS observable).

Node.js error-first convention: fs.readFile supplies an Error or null as the first callback argument, making failure delivery explicit; util.promisify is the deliberate bridge when composition is needed.
React class state commit callback: setState(nextState, callback) invokes the callback after the update commits; it is a completion hook, not the updater function that computes the next state.
Qt event delivery: the event loop calls QObject::event and routes to widget handlers; posted events are deferred while sendEvent is immediate, so the chosen API determines callback timing.

Event-loop bridge in C libraries: libcurl's multi interface drives embedding through two registered callbacks — CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION reports which sockets to poll and CURLMOPT_TIMERFUNCTION reports the timeout — invoked repeatedly, at any time, even after all transfers complete or during cleanup; the contract forces the embedder to keep its context alive until teardown.

Tagged completion demultiplexing: the gRPC C++ async API starts non-blocking RPCs against one CompletionQueue, each bound to a unique void* tag; CompletionQueue::Next(&tag, &ok) delivers every operation's terminal event with an ok flag, so the tag is the callback's context and the queue is the dispatcher.

Result-typed completion handlers: Apple's guidance for failable asynchronous Swift APIs is to return Void and deliver Result<Success, Failure> to a completion handler, because an error raised after the initiating call returned cannot propagate to the caller through throws.
avoid_when: The work is synchronous and there is no framework or event boundary: return a value or use an out parameter; a callback only obscures control flow.
The workflow chains multiple asynchronous steps or needs shared error propagation, timeout, retry, cancellation or fan-in: use a Future/Promise, async/await or coroutine rather than nested callbacks.

The same event must reach multiple independent subscribers with explicit registration, unregistration or fan-out policy: use Observer, EventEmitter or Publisher-Subscriber; a lone callback does not define that policy.

Ordering, backpressure, buffering or delivery guarantees are part of correctness: use a channel or queue such as Point-to-Point Channel, a Go/Rust channel or Polling Consumer; callbacks alone leave those semantics implicit.

The producer cannot push progress or the consumer needs to inspect status, await completion or resume after cancellation: expose a Future/Promise or handle that can be polled or awaited instead of a callback with unspecified lifetime.

A callback may fire both inline and later, or its invocation cardinality cannot be stated: redesign the API or choose separate synchronous/deferred and one-shot/repeated interfaces; documenting ambiguity is not enough.

The consumer needs a linear sequence of transformations and typed composition: async/await or Future/Promise keeps values and failures in the chain; raw callback CPS becomes a pyramid beyond a small boundary adapter.
anti_patterns: Zalgo: calling a callback inline on one branch and later on another makes control flow and reentrancy unpredictable; instead choose one timing contract per API.
Callback of one: passing a callback for a direct result adds inversion of control and hides errors; instead return the value or a Future/Promise.
Fire-and-forget registration: retaining self/this and never unregistering leaks the subscriber graph; instead keep an unsubscribe handle and detach during teardown.
Pyramid of doom: nesting callbacks for sequential operations multiplies indentation and error paths; instead compose a Future/Promise or coroutine.
Error loss: omitting the failure argument or swallowing a callback exception leaves the initiator unaware; instead make failure delivery part of the signature and handle it at the boundary.

Unchecked context: invoking a callback with a raw pointer or captured owner after teardown causes use-after-free or stale mutation; instead tie context lifetime to cancellation and unregister before destruction.
Multiple completion: success and error, or a retry, invoke the terminal callback twice and duplicate side effects; instead guard and detach the callback on the first terminal path.
Anonymous callback capture: putting a large workflow in an inline closure hides ownership and makes testing difficult; instead name the callback or move composition into a separate function.

Synchronous exception crossing async boundary: letting a callback throw through a dispatcher or C ABI escapes the initiating stack and may terminate the process; instead catch at the boundary and route failure through the contract.
design_principles: Inversion of control (Hollywood principle): the service decides when the supplied code runs; the client only supplies it.
Separation of concerns: initiating work, performing work and deciding what to do with the result are separate responsibilities.
Dependency inversion: the service depends on an abstract callback signature, not on concrete client types.
Information hiding: callback plus context lets the client keep its state private while still receiving the result.
Single responsibility per participant: the executor executes, the dispatcher schedules, the callback decides.
Loose coupling: the same service is reused with a different behaviour supplied per call.

Error-as-first-argument convention (Node.js style): the error parameter comes first so callers cannot accidentally omit the error check; this convention has become a de facto standard for callback APIs.

Exactly-once terminal completion: each logical operation produces one terminal callback invocation (success or failure), never both or multiple times; repeated event callbacks need a separate cardinality contract.
best_practices: Write the invocation contract down: when the callback runs (once? per event?), on which thread/loop, what it may do (no blocking, no throwing across the boundary), and what happens on error, cancellation and late completion.
Choose exactly one timing contract per API—always inline or always deferred; if deferred, use the dispatcher so callers never have to defend against two orders.
Carry per-operation state in the callback's own context (closure, delegate target, void* argument) instead of shared fields or globals, one context per in-flight operation.
Give the client a handle to cancel or unregister, define the post-cancel guarantee (no further invocations), and detach the callback when the operation finishes.
Make failures part of the callback signature (errback, status argument, failed path) and guarantee exactly one terminal invocation per operation — success or failure, never both and never none.
Never block inside a callback: hand slow work to a worker or queue so the dispatcher stays free and other completions are not delayed.
Move to futures, async/await or coroutines as soon as the workflow has more than one step, and keep raw callbacks for the single terminal completion or the event-handler boundary.
Watch ownership at registration time: weak references (WeakMethod, WeakReference, [weak self]) for callbacks that outlive their target, and unsubscribe during the owner's teardown.

Distinguish synchronous from asynchronous callbacks: sync callbacks run during the call (Array.map, sort); async callbacks are scheduled on the event loop and run later — mixing them in the same API creates the Zalgo hazard.
Name callbacks rather than using anonymous functions: named functions improve stack traces, enable reuse, and make the code self-documenting.
Handle every error in every callback: use a linter (e.g. eslint callback-return, handle-callback-err) to enforce this; in Node.js, adopt the error-first convention for all new APIs.

Detach the callback from its context on the first invocation: set the stored reference to null or use a oneshot registration so the context can be garbage collected and late spurious invocations are impossible.

When bridging callbacks to promises, use a utility (util.promisify in Node, Promise constructor in JavaScript) and ensure the error-first convention is respected; never resolve and reject the same promise.
For parallel fan-in with callbacks, use a counter or accumulator pattern and define what happens on partial failure — decide whether to fail fast or wait for all completions.
Prefer EventEmitter/Observer semantics when the same event fires multiple times; use a callback only when exactly one completion is expected.

related_patterns_notes.observer: defines repeated notification to registered observers; a callback is only the function one observer may receive.
related_patterns_notes.asynchronous-completion-token: correlates an asynchronous operation with its completion context; callback is the invoked code, while the token carries identity and state.
related_patterns_notes.future-promise: represents one eventual result as a value that can be composed; a callback receives the result directly and does not provide chaining semantics.
related_patterns_notes.command: packages a request as an object for queuing or replay; a callback supplies behavior for an executor without necessarily representing a request.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: fixes an algorithm skeleton in a base class and calls override hooks; a callback injects behavior without inheritance.
related_patterns_notes.reactor: waits for readiness and dispatches handlers; callback is the handler mechanism, while Reactor defines the demultiplexing loop.
related_patterns_notes.proactor: starts asynchronous work and dispatches a completion handler after it finishes; callback is the handler mechanism, while Proactor defines completion-driven scheduling.
related_patterns_notes.publisher-subscriber: defines broker-mediated fan-out to decoupled subscribers; a callback may implement a subscriber but does not define the delivery policy.
related_patterns_notes.continuation-passing-style: represents the rest of a computation as a callback and threads control through it; a callback can be only a local completion hook.
